A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same League of LLMs research. Their complete main text, figures, tables, and Appendices A–G support reliable comparison, including matching renumbered tables.

before.justification: v3 reports original mutual-evaluation experiments with eight LLMs in mathematics and programming, including scores, statistical analyses, ranking stability, and case studies.

after.justification: v4 retains these original experiments and adds reference-answer ablation, sparse Elo replay, question-originality analysis, and resource-consumption results.

M1.justification: Section 8 Q5 introduces League Memory, which filters and regenerates questions using similarity to historical questions, and seasonal topic rotation. These extend question generation, while the core pipeline and Appendix G prompts remain unchanged. Their use in the retained main experiments is not established.

E1.justification: Section 8 Q4 newly uses benchmark question corpora for an originality audit, including GSM8K, which v3 only discussed as prior work. Mathematics and programming remain the capability-evaluation domains; no broader domain evaluation is added.

E2.justification: Section 6 retains the same ranking comparisons with MATH500, AIME2024, Chatbot Arena Math, LiveCodeBench, HumanEval, and Chatbot Arena Coding. The added analyses test LOL variants or question similarity without adding an independent competing evaluation method.

E3.justification: Section 8 adds distinct evaluation protocols: withholding evaluator reference answers, reconstructing Elo rankings from 1%–50% of the comparison pool, and measuring lexical and embedding similarity using 9,322 mathematics and 1,219 programming benchmark questions. This substantially expands evaluation design; the main experiments' models, temperature, and scoring settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses test dependence on reference answers (Q1), ranking robustness under sparse comparisons (Q3), and generated-question overlap with existing benchmarks (Q4). These materially extend validation beyond v3's retained ranking-stability analyses and case studies, although the reference-answer ablation is reported only qualitatively.

E5.justification: v4 reports 100 independent random-sampling repetitions for the new sparse Elo replay. This does not increase the five runs of the retained main experiments. Existing confidence intervals, dispersion statistics, and significance-testing procedures remain unchanged; uncertainty intervals for the new replay results are not supplied.

E6.justification: The original scores, rankings, and appendix statistics are unchanged, but v4 substantially expands reported findings. Additions include largely preserved rankings without reference answers; replay correlations of 1.00 for mathematics and 0.93 for programming at 30% comparisons; respective 5-gram overlaps of 5.11% and 5.90% and semantic similarities of 0.4856 and 0.5730; and token-consumption and cost results. These are new analyses, not same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: The mathematical example and reference derivation in Appendix F and the statistical definitions in the appendices are retained. The additions introduce no new theorem, proof, formal assumption, or mathematical derivation.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's empirical contribution, and conclusion replace the claim of significant OpenAI-family homophily bias with the narrower observation of higher in-family scores. The underlying difference and significance remain unchanged, as do the central paradigm and ranking claims.

C2.justification: Finding 5 newly acknowledges OpenAI models' reasoning strength as a possible explanation for higher in-family scores. Added discussion interprets replay and similarity results as supporting scalability and originality. The limitations also soften the explicit warning about API cost, latency, and rapidly growing interaction overhead while adding concern about question diversity.

D1.justification: New Table 1 discloses per-model input/output token consumption for both domains, and Q3 reports average experiment costs of $1.87 for mathematics and $3.29 for programming. Q4 identifies all-MiniLM-L6-v2 for similarity analysis. Existing API settings, prompts, and code-access information remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v4 adds Wang et al. (2020), MiniLM, for the embedding analysis. Section 7 also adopts the narrower in-family-score terminology, while retaining the positioning of LOL against single-model LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation.

P1.justification: The discussion expands from two questions to five, acknowledgments are added, and bias terminology is revised across several sections and Appendix E. Most prose and the overall section sequence remain unchanged.

P2.justification: v4 adds a full-width token-consumption table, renumbers the six existing tables, and revises the developer-family table caption. Existing Figures 1–16 are retained without substantive visual changes; surrounding text and appendix tables undergo limited layout reflow.

improvement.justification: v4 improves claim calibration by distinguishing higher in-family scores from demonstrated bias, and adds useful validation and cost information in Section 8 and Table 1. The gains are limited by qualitative ablation reporting, sparse replay that does not directly measure realized operational savings, and unvalidated question-diversity mechanisms with unspecified settings. Despite stronger scalability language and softened cost caveats, the added transparency and more cautious bias interpretation provide a modest net improvement.
